title: Confidence intervals and significance
summary: A percentile bootstrap confidence interval shows the range of plausible values for an effect; whether it excludes zero answers significance, its location answers relevance.

body.text: A 95% [[percentile-interval]] consists of the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the bootstrap estimates. If it excludes zero, the effect is significant at the 5% level in a two-sided test. SEM Studio also reports a [[p-value]] from the bootstrap t statistic (estimate / SE).

body.explanation: θ̂⁽ᵇ⁾ (b = 1 … B) are the B bootstrap estimates of a parameter θ, and q₀.₀₂₅ and q₀.₉₇₅ their 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles.

body.text: In the TAM example PEOU → BI = .128 with 95% CI [.047, .210] (5,000 draws, seed 20261103): significantly positive, but plausibly anywhere from very small to modest. Significance is not importance: report the estimate and its interval and judge the size in context (Wasserstein & Lazar 2016).

Bias-corrected and accelerated ([[bca-interval]]) intervals adjust for bias and skewness of the bootstrap distribution. SEM Studio does not compute them yet; it offers percentile intervals. One-sided tests are appropriate only for a directional hypothesis stated before seeing the data.

mistake.title: Equating "significant" with "important"
mistake.text: With a large sample a trivial effect can be significant, and with a small sample an important one may not be. An interval that includes zero does not show that the effect is zero either.

tryIt.task: Run the TAM example and read the 95% intervals of the three paths. Which interval is the widest relative to its estimate?

checks.question: PEOU → BI = .128, 95% CI [.047, .210]. Which interpretation is best?

options.text: The effect is positive and significant at 5%, and the data are consistent with values from about .05 to .21.
options.feedback: Correct. The interval conveys both direction and the range of plausible sizes.

options.text: There is a 95% probability that the true effect is exactly .128.
options.feedback: The point estimate is one value; the interval, not the estimate, expresses uncertainty, and frequentist intervals do not assign probabilities to fixed parameters.
A confidence interval quantifies sampling uncertainty under the model; it does not establish causation.

options.text: The effect is large because it is significant.
options.feedback: Significance says nothing about size; .128 is small to modest.

checks.explanation: Read both the location and the width of the interval.

checks.question: Another path is .14 with 95% CI [−.02, .30]. What may you conclude?

options.text: It is not significant at 5%, and the data are compatible with a zero, a small negative or a moderate positive effect.
options.feedback: Correct. Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.
The interval also includes .30. Non-significance does not show the effect is zero.
A 95% interval does not tell you directly about the 10% level; you would need the 90% interval or the p value.
